p.title: The Kernel of Truth in Text-Based Personality Assessment: A Meta-Analysis of the Relations Between the Big Five and the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)

ext.title: The Kernel of Truth in Text-Based Personality Assessment: A Meta-Analysis of the Relations Between the Big Five and the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)
ext.venue: Psychological Bulletin, 148(11-12), 843-868. Correction to metadata hint: the hint said 2024; the PDF gives 2022 (received April 8, 2022; accepted November 2, 2022).
ext.coverage: Read the full extracted text (all 4,110 lines, front matter through the reference list and receipt dates). Full coverage of the abstract, introduction, method, results (Tables 2-6 and Figure 3), discussion, limitations, conclusion and references. The paper contains no content on lobbying, legislators, networks, path-finding, allocation, or persuasion/turnout. Elections appear only as one included study task (Abe, 2018, reflection on U.S. elections; Table 2). Text measurement is covered in depth (LIWC closed-vocabulary method). Paul's markup: no files were listed for this PDF, and a search of /_annots for the document hash 694a803d85d2 returned no matches, so no markup was read or reported. Page numbers come from the running heads in the text dump and may be off by one in places; section and table locations are exact.
ext.research_question: Do self-reported and observer-reported Big Five traits correlate with the 52 LIWC categories shared across LIWC2001, LIWC2007 and LIWC2015 (cue validity and cue utilization)? Which categories form a "kernel of truth" that both self- and observer-reports link to? Do 10 study, sample and task moderators explain heterogeneity in these effects? (Introduction, pp. 843-847.)
ext.theory: Brunswik's (1955) lens model (cue validity vs cue utilization); Realistic Accuracy Model (Funder, 1995, 2012) for the kernel-of-truth idea; Self-Other Knowledge Asymmetry model (Vazire, 2010), which predicts observer reports will show larger effects for overt behavior such as verbal behavior; Trait Activation Theory (Tett and Guterman, 2000; Tett et al., 2021), used for predictions on language formality and task synchronicity; "words as attention" account of word use (Tausczik and Pennebaker, 2010).
ext.data: 31 eligible samples from 26 studies (k = 31 samples, 26 studies), total N = 85,724 participants. Unit of analysis: sample/study-level correlations between Big Five trait scores and LIWC category scores. Cue validity: 26 self-report samples (Table 3 note reports k = 25, n = 83,243-84,084 for the analysed effects; Schwartz et al., 2013 alone has n = 72,809). Cue utilization: 5 observer-report samples (Table 3 note: n = 1,637). Mean age 27.96 years (SD 10.50) for cue validity samples; 23.66 (SD 5.52) for cue utilization. Text length >40 words required. Period: literature searched September 8-10, 2020, from 1999 onward (LIWC publication year). Eligible: healthy English-speaking adults; LIWC2022 excluded because it was published after the search. Screening: 691 database records plus 22 additional records; 429 abstracts screened; 124 full texts; 26 studies included (Figure 2, p. 849). Missing data: 12% of values imputed (see method).
ext.method: PRISMA-reported systematic review followed by meta-analysis (random-effects model, R package "meta"). Effect size: Pearson r, Fisher z transformation and back-transformation; Spearman rho converted to r for one study. Corrected effects (rho) disattenuated for personality-measure reliability only (Cronbach alpha for self-reports; ICC for observer reports); LIWC categories not corrected. Missing effect sizes (12% of values) imputed with a self-devised "mean minus 1" rule (sum of available effects plus zeros, divided by k-1); analyses based on this rule (pp. 847-849). Heterogeneity: Cochran Q, I2, tau. Publication bias: Egger's test on uncorrected, nonimputed data. Moderators (five categorical: LIWC version, written-spoken, formality, synchronicity, sample composition; five continuous: sample size, text length, age, percentage women, publication year) tested with meta-regression. Explained variance per trait: meta-analytic linear regression of each trait on all LIWC categories in lavaan, using a 52-category weighted average correlation matrix from 14 studies (n = 6,405) and the harmonic mean n. Content vs function words analysed separately, using narrow categories only to avoid double counting. Two coders per study (first author coded all; four research assistants coded a quarter each).
ext.identification: None in the econometric sense. This is a correlational meta-analysis. Cue validity is the correlation between self-reports and LIWC categories; cue utilization is the correlation between observer reports and LIWC categories; the "kernel of truth" is the set of categories significant in the same direction for both (Figure 1). The authors explicitly state that "valid cues" does not mean "true" personality.
ext.scope: Population: healthy adults writing or speaking English (mostly students and general-population samples, US-centric social media). Era: studies from 1999 to 2020, LIWC2001, LIWC2007 and LIWC2015 only. Instrument scope: the 52 LIWC categories shared by these versions; Big Five (plus HEXACO Emotionality/Agreeableness treated as Big Five, one study). HEXACO Honesty-Humility not reported (single study). Text types: blogs, Facebook/Twitter posts, essays, dreams, interviews, daily speech (EAR), chats. Results are English-specific (p. 861).

key_findings.finding: Self-reported traits correlate significantly with LIWC categories, but effects are small. Strongest |rho| ranged .08-.14; the 52 categories explain on average 5.1% of self-reported personality variance.
key_findings.numbers: |rho| = .08-.14; mean R2 = 5.07% (cue validity, narrow categories, Table 4)

key_findings.finding: Observer-reported traits correlate with LIWC categories with small-to-medium effects, explaining much more variance than self-reports.
key_findings.location: Abstract, p. 843; Results, Cue Utilization, pp. 852-853; Table 4, p. 854
key_findings.numbers: |rho| = .18-.39; mean R2 = 38.52% (cue utilization); Emotional Stability lowest at 31.48%, Conscientiousness highest at 47.32%

key_findings.finding: Cue validity effects for individual categories (Table 3). Examples: Openness with words longer than six letters rho = .11; Conscientiousness with negative emotions rho = -.12, swear words -.11, anger -.10; Agreeableness with anger -.14, swear -.10, negative emotions -.10, positive emotions .10; Emotional Stability with negative emotions -.12. No Extraversion category reached |rho| >= .10.
key_findings.location: Results, Cue Validity, p. 852; Table 3, pp. 852-853
key_findings.numbers: As listed; k = 25 samples, n = 83,243-84,084 (Table 3 note)

key_findings.finding: Cue utilization effects for individual categories (Table 3). Examples: Agreeableness with swear words rho = -.39; Conscientiousness with swear words -.35, anger -.32, negative emotions -.30, sexual -.29; Extraversion with word count .31; Openness with word count .18 and leisure .17; Emotional Stability with first-person singular pronouns -.29.

Kernel of truth: 20 of 260 linguistic markers (5 traits x 52 categories) were significant in the same direction for both self- and observer-reports (3 Openness, 4 Conscientiousness, 3 Extraversion, 4 Agreeableness, 6 Emotional Stability). Eight reached |rho| >= .10; four also had lower 95% CI >= .05 (Conscientiousness: swear, anger, negative emotions; Agreeableness: swear). Across the 20 markers, cue validity and utilization correlate r = .94; across all 260, r = .52. Four markers pointed in opposite directions.
key_findings.location: Results, Kernel of Truth, p. 853; Figure 3, p. 853; Discussion, pp. 856-857
key_findings.numbers: 20/260; r = .94 (20 markers); r = .52 (all 260); 8 at |rho| >= .10; 4 with lower CI >= .05

key_findings.finding: Cue utilization was larger than cue validity in both effect sizes and explained variance, consistent with the Self-Other Knowledge Asymmetry model.
key_findings.location: Discussion, Self-Other Knowledge Asymmetry Model, p. 857

key_findings.finding: Function words explained little variance but were valid and utilized markers for some traits; content words explained more.
key_findings.location: Results, Explained Variance, p. 853; Discussion, Other Findings: Function Words, p. 858; Table 4, p. 854
key_findings.numbers: Cue validity: function 1.31%, content 3.71%. Cue utilization: function 5.05%, content 28.68%.

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity was pervasive and moderators explained part of it. Significant heterogeneity in 96% of cue-validity and 82% of cue-utilization effects; the 10 moderators explained some heterogeneity in 70% and 61% of effects.

Language formality: low-Agreeableness individuals used more swear words in informal settings (rho = -.14) than formal (rho = -.07), a significant difference (QM = 4.64, p = .03), as TAT predicted. Synchronicity did not moderate Extraversion and positive emotion (synchronous rho = .07 vs asynchronous .01; QM = 1.03, p = .31), so the Chen et al. (2020) finding was not replicated.
key_findings.location: Results, Categorical Moderators, p. 854; Discussion, Regarding TAT, p. 858
key_findings.numbers: rho -.14 informal vs -.07 formal (QM = 4.64, p = .03); QM = 1.03, p = .31

key_findings.finding: Text mode: Extraversion with word count was much stronger for spoken than written language.
key_findings.location: Results, Categorical Moderators, p. 854; Table 5, p. 855
key_findings.numbers: Spoken rho = .23 vs written .03 (word count, Extraversion)

key_findings.finding: LIWC version: older versions produced larger average effects.
key_findings.location: Results, Categorical Moderators, p. 854; Discussion, p. 857

key_findings.finding: Continuous moderators: effects were typically stronger for longer texts and weaker for larger samples. Negative-valence associations for Conscientiousness and Agreeableness (swear, anger, negative emotions) and for Emotional Stability (negative emotions) weakened with publication year.
key_findings.location: Results, Continuous Moderators, p. 854; Table 6, p. 856; Discussion, p. 858
key_findings.numbers: Year-of-publication slopes significant for Agreeableness swear and anger and Emotional Stability negative emotions (cue validity, Table 6); sample size b < .001 for many cue-utilization effects

key_findings.finding: Publication bias: Egger tests flagged 99 of 260 cue-validity and 11 of 260 cue-utilization effects; excluding Schwartz et al. (2013) left 6. The authors argue small-study effects do not indicate publication bias because effects did not shrink with sample size and were smaller without Schwartz.

Benchmark against other methods. The strongest LIWC category per trait beat human judges for most traits but lagged computer methods (Moreno et al., 2021; IBM-WPI; HTTP). Average LIWC correlation in the table was .10 (self) and .25 (observer), versus .12 for human judges (Tskhay and Rule, 2014) and .27-.31 for other computer methods.
key_findings.location: Discussion, LIWC Versus Other Methods, pp. 858-860; Table 7, p. 859; Future Research, p. 861
key_findings.numbers: Average r: LIWC .10 (self) / .25 (observer); human judges .12; Moreno et al. (2021) .27; IBM-WPI .13; HTTP .31 (uncorrected)

measures: LIWC (LIWC2001, LIWC2007, LIWC2015): 52 categories shared across versions; word count, dictionary, words >6 letters, function-word and affect categories, and others (Table 1)
Big Five traits via self-report inventories (BFI-44, TIPI-10, IPIP-20/50/100/300, NEO-FFI, BFAS-100, HEXACO-PI-R; Table 2) and observer ratings (acquaintances, strangers, Facebook-based ratings)
Effect size: Pearson r (Fisher z pooled), corrected to rho for personality reliability (Cronbach alpha or ICC)
Explained variance R2 (%) per trait from meta-analytic regression across LIWC categories
Heterogeneity: Cochran Q, I2, tau; publication bias: Egger test
limitations: Corrected effects are probably underestimates: LIWC categories were not disattenuated for their reliability (authors argue they are formative measures; Limitations, p. 860).
Cue utilization rests on only k = 5 samples (vs 26 for cue validity), so categorical moderators could not be tested for it and the kernel of truth is probably underestimated (p. 861).
The cue-validity pool is dominated by Schwartz et al. (2013), n = 72,809 (the authors ran analyses with and without it).

12% of effect-size and moderator values were missing; missingness was non-random (non-significant effects were often unreported). The authors used a self-devised 'mean minus 1' imputation, which they admit may distort true effects (pp. 847-849).
Observer reports were mostly zero-acquaintance, and only one study used acquaintances; the acquaintance effect could not be tested (p. 861).
Several studies were small, and the authors note only large effects reach significance in small samples (p. 862).
Test-retest reliability was not used, because repeating verbal tasks can change responses (p. 860).
Results are English-specific, and LIWC has not been designed for personality assessment; Table 7 comparisons use each method's best category and are post hoc (footnote 9, p. 859).
Language formality and synchronicity are broad classifications, which may have attenuated situational moderation (p. 858).
Honesty-Humility is not covered (single study, Holtrop et al., 2019).
Egger's test flagged many cue-validity effects; the authors argue this reflects small-study effects rather than publication bias, which is a judgment call (p. 854).
references_of_note: Abe, J. A. A. (2018). Personality and political preferences: The 2016 U.S. Presidential Election. Journal of Research in Personality, 77, 70-82. Included study; task was reflection on upcoming U.S. elections (Table 2, p. 851). Only election-related item in the paper.

Schwartz, H. A., et al. (2013). Personality, gender, and age in the language of social media: The open-vocabulary approach. PLOS ONE, 8(9), e73791. Facebook MyPersonality data, n = 72,809; drives cue-validity results.

Eichstaedt, J. C., et al. (2021). Closed- and open-vocabulary approaches to text analysis: A review, quantitative comparison, and recommendations. Psychological Methods, 26(4), 398-427. Comparative benchmark for closed vs open vocabulary methods.
Park, G., et al. (2015). Automatic personality assessment through social media language. JPSP, 108(6), 934-952. Open-vocabulary benchmark; test-retest comparison cited in Conclusion.

Mairesse, F., et al. (2007). Using linguistic cues for the automatic recognition of personality in conversation and text. JAIR, 30, 457-500. Source of the PersonalityRecognizer tool built on LIWC categories; reanalysed Pennebaker and King data.

Holtzman, N. S., et al. (2019). Linguistic markers of grandiose narcissism: A LIWC analysis of 15 samples. Journal of Language and Social Psychology, 38(5-6), 773-786. Prior LIWC meta-level moderator comparison.

Chen, J., Qiu, L., & Ho, M. H. R. (2020). A meta-analysis of linguistic markers of extraversion: Positive emotion and social process words. Journal of Research in Personality, 89. Prior LIWC meta-analysis; source of the synchronicity moderator hypothesis.
Holtrop, D. J., et al. (2022). Exploring the application of text-to-personality algorithms in job interviews. EJWOP, 31(6). HTTP closed-vocabulary tool; comparison benchmark.

Hickman, L., Tay, L., & Woo, S. E. (2019). Validity evidence for off-the-shelf language-based personality assessment using video interviews. Personnel Assessment and Decisions, 5(3). IBM-WPI validity failure in job interviews.

Moreno, J. D., et al. (2021). Can personality traits be measured analyzing written language? A meta-analytic study on computational methods. Personality and Individual Differences, 177. Computational text-personality meta-analysis benchmark.
Tskhay, K. O., & Rule, N. O. (2014). Perceptions of personality in text-based media and OSN: A meta-analysis. JRP, 49, 25-30. Human-judge accuracy benchmark (r = .12).
Vazire, S. (2010). Who knows what about a person? The self-other knowledge asymmetry (SOKA) model. JPSP, 98(2), 281-300. Theoretical basis for cue-utilization > cue-validity prediction.
Funder, D. C. (1995). On the accuracy of personality judgment: A realistic approach. Psychological Review, 102(4), 652-670. RAM underpinning the kernel-of-truth concept.
Tausczik, Y. R., & Pennebaker, J. W. (2010). The psychological meaning of words: LIWC and computerized text analysis methods. JLSP, 29(1), 24-54. Core LIWC methods reference.

Qiu, L., Lin, H., Ramsay, J., & Yang, F. (2012). You are what you tweet: Personality expression and perception on Twitter. JRP, 46(6), 710-718. Included Twitter study (cue validity and utilization); Twitter-based personality expression.
Golbeck, J., Robles, C., Edmondson, M., & Turner, K. (2011). Predicting personality from Twitter. IEEE PASSAT/SocialCom. Included prediction study on social media text.

short_quotes.quote: self-reported personality traits are significantly correlated with linguistic categories, but the effect sizes are relatively small
the LIWC categories serve as linguistic markers of personality traits
cue utilization was larger than cue validity, both in terms of effect sizes and explained variance
short_quotes.location: Discussion, Self-Other Knowledge Asymmetry Model, p. 857

rel.summary_md:
Koutsoumpis et al. (Psychological Bulletin, 2022; the vault slug says 2024, the PDF says 2022) pooled 31 samples (N = 85,724). They correlated Big Five scores with the 52 LIWC categories shared by LIWC2001, 2007 and 2015.

**Self-reports (cue validity), 26 samples.** Effects are small. The strongest correlations run |rho| .08-.14, and all 52 categories together explain about 5.1% of trait variance.

**Observer ratings (cue utilization), only 5 samples (n = 1,637).** Effects are larger: |rho| .18-.39, with R2 averaging 38.5%.

**Overlap.** Only 20 of 260 trait-by-category markers agree in direction for both self and observer reports. The paper calls this the "kernel of truth". Examples: swear words, anger and negative emotion for low Conscientiousness and low Agreeableness, and negative emotion for low Emotional Stability.

**Other results.** Heterogeneity is nearly universal: 96% of self-report effects and 82% of observer effects. Formal settings weaken some markers, for example Agreeableness with swear words is -.07 formal vs -.14 informal. Spoken text carries much more Extraversion signal through word count than written text (.23 vs .03). LIWC also trails other computer methods (.10 vs .27-.31).

**Why it matters for Melange.** The system's lexical Big Five (`big5_traits.py`) is this closed-vocabulary method applied to formal congressional speech. It uses short published-exemplar word lists, not licensed LIWC dictionaries. The paper sets a low ceiling on how much true trait signal such rates can carry. That supports four existing choices: the brain's reading that the RKH convergence (CV mean .350) is inflated by shared method, retiring the lexical basis from the receptivity layer, square-root token shrinkage, and keeping status labels on any external claim.

The paper also gives a direction check for the active SMOreg weights, and some of them point the opposite way. Finally, observer-panel passes need care. The paper says plainly that valid cues are not the same as true personality, so convergence with the Senate expert panels may partly reflect raters using the same cues the text model uses (utilization), not validity.

bearings.paper_claim: Self-reported Big Five correlate with LIWC categories at most |rho| .08-.14. All 52 categories together explain a mean R2 of 5.07% of self-reported trait variance (narrow categories; k = 25, n about 83-84k, dominated by Schwartz et al. 2013, n = 72,809). Heterogeneity is significant in 96% of these effects. LIWC's average best-category r of .10 trails other computer methods (.27-.31).
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p. 843; Discussion p. 854; Table 4 p. 854; Table 7 p. 859
bearings.system_side: The component z-scores per-1000-word closed-vocabulary rates (LIWC-analog exemplar lists plus the Empath overlay, MATTR and concreteness) within this corpus. It combines them with linear weights; the essays-fitted SMOreg weights are active when the json file is present, then refit to RKH. Reported held-out CV vs RKH has mean .350 (E .510). RKH is itself Mairesse-LIWC text-derived, per brain topics/2026-07-feature-personality-psychometrics.md:51.
bearings.transfer_conditions: These are adult general-population and student samples, mostly informal social media, LIWC 2001-2015, in English. Congressional floor speech and interviews are formal and partly staff-written. The paper shows formality attenuates markers (Agreeableness-swear -.14 informal vs -.07 formal). The system uses short exemplar lists (swear = 'damn hell crap'), not licensed LIWC dictionaries, so category equivalence is unverified. Read the paper as an upper bound on true trait signal from closed-vocabulary rates. A text-vs-RKH convergence of .35 therefore cannot be read as trait validity, which agrees with the brain's method-shared caveat.

bearings.paper_claim: Kernel and per-trait directions in the paper: Emotional Stability relates negatively to negative-emotion words (cue validity rho -.12) and to first-person singular pronouns (cue utilization rho -.29). Agreeableness relates negatively to anger (-.14) and swear words (-.10). Conscientiousness relates negatively to swear words (-.11) and anger (-.10). Openness relates positively to words longer than six letters (.11).
bearings.paper_location: Results, Cue Validity and Cue Utilization, pp. 852-853; Table 3; Figure 3 p. 853
bearings.system_side: The active SMOreg weights replace the published-correlate W. Several agree with the paper: Agreeableness anger -.0202 and swear -.0323, Conscientiousness anger -.0556 and swear -.0446, Openness sixltr +.0292. Others run the opposite way or are near zero: ES on first-person singular +.0094 (the paper's direction is negative), ES on negative emotion -.0002 (near zero), and E on positive emotion -.0339 (the literature direction is positive). The hand-set fallback W at lines 180-181 had the paper's signs.
bearings.transfer_conditions: SMOreg weights are multivariate, so suppression can legitimately flip a weight's sign relative to a bivariate correlation. The paper's estimates are bivariate. Treat this as a direction audit flag, not proof of error. It carries over only if the exemplar categories behave like LIWC categories. This comparison is my own single-path analysis and stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Observer-rated traits correlate much more strongly with LIWC than self-reports do: R2 38.52% vs 5.07%, and |rho| up to .39 (Agreeableness-swear) and .31 (Extraversion-word count). This fits the Self-Other Knowledge Asymmetry model. The authors stress that valid or utilized cues do not equal 'true' personality. Observers were mostly zero-acquaintance raters judging the same text cues. Emotional Stability had the lowest observer R2 (31.48%).
bearings.paper_location: Results, Cue Utilization pp. 852-853; Table 4 p. 854; Discussion, Self-Other Knowledge Asymmetry Model p. 857; Limitations p. 861
bearings.system_side: Text traits are tested against the 'Personality on the Hill' Senate panels (129 insiders, 125 academics), which are observer ratings. E and A pass both panels, O passes academics only, N passes insiders only, and C shows an insider association only. A-ES of about .44 is read as population-real plus about .21 text-tone halo.
bearings.code_ref: C:/Users/pgoff/Documents/brain/topics/2026-07-feature-personality-psychometrics.md:52 (fec/big5_improvements_eval.py, listed in the component, was not found at that path)
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's observer samples are k = 5 with n = 1,637, nearly all zero-acquaintance. The Senate panels are informed experts and insiders, which the paper could not test. SOKA predicts panel passes for E and A, the overt traits, and weakest results for ES, and that matches the system. Because utilization can reflect shared stereotypes, panel convergence supports 'raters and text use the same cues' more than trait accuracy. That backs the system's rule that status labels accompany any external claim.

bearings.paper_claim: Emotional Stability relates negatively to negative-emotion words (cue validity rho -.12) and to first-person singular (cue utilization rho -.29). Emotional Stability carries 6 of the 20 kernel markers. Negative-valence associations weaken with publication year, and effects vary by text mode and setting.
bearings.paper_location: Results, Kernel of Truth p. 853; Table 3; Table 6 p. 856; Discussion p. 858
bearings.system_side: The LIWC anchor is z(first-person singular) + z(negemo) - z(posemo) on interview text of 800 words or more. Since round-7b it is only the convergent-validity anchor (gate G3, r = +.24), not a component. The measure is the E-residualized, party-controlled LLM affective-N. Genre transfer to floor and hearing text failed (rho .050, .161).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports the anchor's sign structure (high-N is more 'I', more negemo, less posemo) and its small expected size, so an anchor r near .24 is plausible. The failed genre transfer is consistent with the paper's pervasive heterogeneity and mode and formality moderators. This is direction support only, not evidence that N predicts yielding under pressure.

bearings.paper_claim: The 52 LIWC categories explain about 5% of self-reported trait variance, and the strongest single markers sit at |rho| of about .10-.14.
bearings.system_side: The default basis is behavioral (RECEPT_TRAITS=behavioral) after the pre-registered nomological test indicted the lexical Big5. The lexical fallback susc = .40A + .30N - .20C - .10E uses graded sqrt(tokens/1500) shrinkage.
bearings.transfer_conditions: With so little true trait variance in closed-vocabulary rates, a susceptibility composite built from them would be mostly noise. That independently supports keeping the lexical basis out of the default. The paper also finds effects strengthen with longer texts, which is consistent with token-based shrinkage, though the sqrt(tokens/1500) form is not estimated by this paper.

gaps_exposed: The lexical reader has no licensed LIWC dictionary: categories are short exemplar lists (swear = 3 words) plus the Empath overlay. The paper's effect sizes are for LIWC dictionaries, and the system has no check that its categories are equivalent.

There is no formality or genre moderator in the lexical model. The paper shows formality and spoken vs written mode change effect sizes (Agreeableness-swear -.14 vs -.07; Extraversion-word count spoken .23 vs written .03). The system pools floor, interview and social text and has already seen genre transfer fail for N.

No sign audit of the fitted SMOreg weights against literature kernel directions. ES on first-person singular and E on positive emotion run opposite to the paper, and ES on negative emotion is near zero.

No open-vocabulary or embedding benchmark: the paper's Table 7 puts other computer methods at r .27-.31 against LIWC's .10 for self-reports. The system's alternative LLM reader is display-only and failed its behavioral diagonal (+0.064).
No cue-validity vs cue-utilization distinction in the validation framing: observer-panel convergence (E, A) is not separated from shared-stereotype cue use.
flags: Metadata: the vault slug and hint say 2024. The paper is Psychological Bulletin 2022, 148(11-12), 843-868, doi 10.1037/bul0000381.

Documentation drift: the component brief says affective_n = z(LIWC) + z(LLM). The live code, emit_affective_n.py:39-43, says LIWC is only the convergent-validity anchor since round-7b, and the measure is the E-residualized, party-controlled LLM affective-N.

The active SMOreg weights (fec/liwc/mairesse_smoreg.json:20, :43, :51) give E a negative weight on positive emotion, ES a positive weight on first-person singular, and ES a near-zero weight on negative emotion, against the paper's directions. This is a multivariate-suppression caveat, not proof of error. UNVERIFIED single-path analysis (DE-062).

Do not quote the RKH held-out CV (.350, E .510) as trait validity. RKH is itself Mairesse-LIWC text-derived, and the paper's 5% ceiling on self-report variance makes method-shared inflation the likely explanation.
Do not read observer-panel passes as trait accuracy. The paper says valid or utilized cues do not mean 'true' personality, and its observer evidence rests on k = 5 mostly zero-acquaintance samples.
No brain wording rule is triggered: the paper does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization, and makes no LDA, reciprocity or influence claims.
rel.paul_alignment:
Paul calls Ramey's closed-vocabulary approach "dated but foundational" and asks for frameworks specific to each venue. Birkenmaier's highlights call Ramey's SVM outdated and unvalidated. This meta-analysis backs both points with numbers. Closed-vocabulary categories explain only about 5% of self-reported trait variance, and venue matters: formality, spoken vs written, and heterogeneity in 96% of effects. So the evidence agrees with his skepticism and with his call for venue-specific frameworks.

His notes are stale relative to the system. They do not record three things:
- The pre-registered nomological test already indicted the lexical Big5 for behavioral prediction, and the receptivity layer now defaults to a behavioral basis (receptivity_layer.py:59-64).
- N now comes from an E-residualized LLM reader, with LIWC only as an anchor.
- RKH convergence is method-shared.

The paper does not support his endorsement of LLM trait reading directly, because it does not test LLMs. It only shows that non-LIWC computer methods reach r of about .27-.31. The system's own LLM reader has not cleared its behavioral bar.

related.why: Ramey et al. apply LIWC/Mairesse closed-vocabulary trait scoring to congressional speech, the RKH source the system calibrates to. This meta-analysis sets the ceiling on how much true trait signal that method can carry.
Pennebaker's 'words as attention' account and the LIWC category design are the theoretical and instrumental base the meta-analysis evaluates.
A parallel meta-analysis of predicting the Big Five from social-media footprints. Its larger pooled effects contrast with LIWC-only effects and frame the open- vs closed-vocabulary gap.
The Senate expert and insider panels the system uses as gold are observer ratings. The paper's cue-utilization vs cue-validity distinction (SOKA) governs how to read text-panel convergence.
Birkenmaier validates computational trait measures for politicians and criticizes Ramey-style SVM. This meta-analysis supplies the quantitative reason closed-vocabulary signal is weak.
Deep-learning text personality models report stronger trait recovery than LIWC categories, consistent with the paper's Table 7 finding that LIWC lags other computer methods.
A Twitter-based study of Emotional Stability linguistic markers. It bears on the paper's six ES kernel markers and on the system's affective-N anchor.
